ui.welcome: Ride along with Bob, a shipping container, from an exporter's warehouse to an importer's door — and back to the depot. Bob tells his own story: who handles him, which documents travel with him, what it costs and what can go wrong. At each step, you decide what happens next.
ui.howto: Choose your level, a container type, a route and an Incoterm. **★ Essential** items must be opened before you can move on. Underlined words open the glossary.
ui.menuNote: All companies, vessels, references and figures are fictional or illustrative. Items marked TO VERIFY must be validated by a qualified colleague before this module is used in production.

ui.incoNote: Incoterms 2020 apply only if the sales contract refers to them, ideally as "[rule] [named place] Incoterms 2020". Named places in this module are examples. [TO VERIFY:v14]

1: Incoterms do **not** transfer ownership of the goods — the sales contract does.
The Incoterm says who pays and who carries the risk — not who owns the container. The container belongs to the carrier (or a leasing company).
FOB and CIF are famous, but for containers ICC recommends FCA and CIP instead. [TO VERIFY:v15]
2: Incoterms do **not** transfer ownership and say nothing about price, payment terms or the B/L type.
They only apply when the contract refers to them, ideally "[rule] [named place] Incoterms 2020".
FOB, CFR and CIF are for goods handed over on board. For containers delivered to a terminal, ICC recommends FCA, CPT or CIP. [TO VERIFY:v15]
C-rules have **two** critical points: risk passes at origin, costs run to destination. Insurance under CIF is minimal cover (ICC C). [TO VERIFY:v18]
The Incoterm does not decide who pays demurrage and detention once delays occur — the contract of carriage and the sales contract do.
3: Using FOB for a container delivered to the terminal days before loading leaves the seller at risk for goods it no longer controls — a classic dispute. [TO VERIFY:v15]
CIF minimum cover (ICC C) excludes many risks (e.g. theft, water damage under some conditions): buyers of high-value goods often need extra cover. [TO VERIFY:v18]
DDP makes the seller the importer of record: a non-EU seller needs EU representation and VAT handling. [TO VERIFY:v26]
EXW makes the buyer responsible for export clearance in a country where it may not be established — use FCA seller's premises instead. [TO VERIFY:v14]
Demurrage, detention and storage after a customs hold are allocated by the contracts, not by the Incoterm — specify them.

intro.text: Hi! I'm **Bob**. 👋 Steel body, 12 metres long, nine and a half feet tall — I'm a 40-foot shipping container. Please don't call me "a box". Okay, you can. Everybody does.
My job? I carry stuff around the planet: fridges, sneakers, bananas, machines… Whatever's inside, I never peek. Professional secret. 🤫
On every trip, dozens of people look after me: bookers, truck drivers, crane drivers, planners, customs officers, finance teams… And starting today, **you**.

Together we'll go through 11 steps, from an empty depot to a customer's door and back. At each step, you decide what happens next. Get it wrong and I'll look like this. Don't worry — I bounce back fast.
First, a few choices: your level, my outfit (the container type), our route, and the deal between seller and buyer — the [[incoterms|Incoterm]]. Ready to ship out?

levels.desc: Plain English, the big picture, 3-option questions with hints.

containers.name: 20' dry
containers.desc: The basic box: 1 TEU, about 33 m³. Dense cargo fills its weight limit before its space. [TO VERIFY:v53]
containers.typical: Tiles, paper reels, machine parts, bagged goods

containers.name: 40' dry
containers.desc: Twice the length of a 20' (2 TEU), about 67 m³, same 8'6" height. [TO VERIFY:v53]

containers.name: 40' high cube
containers.desc: One foot taller (9'6"), about 76 m³: the workhorse for light, bulky goods. [TO VERIFY:v05]

containers.name: 40' reefer
containers.desc: Insulated box with its own refrigeration unit: plugged in at terminals and on board, temperature monitored all the way. [TO VERIFY:v53]

containers.name: 40' open top
containers.desc: No rigid roof: loaded from above by crane, covered by a tarpaulin. Cargo taller than the box is out-of-gauge (OOG). [TO VERIFY:v53]
containers.typical: Tall machinery, glass, heavy items lifted by crane

containers.name: 40' flat rack
containers.desc: Floor and end walls only, for heavy or out-of-gauge cargo that needs special lashing and stowage. No doors, so no door seal. [TO VERIFY:v53]

containers.name: 20' tank
containers.desc: A stainless-steel tank in a 20' frame for liquids, often dangerous goods under the [[imdg]]. Owned mostly by tank operators. [TO VERIFY:v53]

routes.name: Shanghai → Le Havre
routes.detail: Mainline service from Shanghai (Yangshan) to Le Havre: about 30–35 days via Suez, 40+ days via the Cape of Good Hope. [TO VERIFY:v10] Ships of 15,000–24,000 TEU are typical. [TO VERIFY:v11]
routes.transit: ≈ 30–35 days via Suez · 40+ via the Cape

compat.reefer: Reefers from Shanghai to Europe exist (frozen seafood, for example), but the classic reefer lanes are fruit lanes such as Ecuador–Europe.

routes.name: Ho Chi Minh City → Singapore → Le Havre
routes.detail: A feeder ship carries the box from Cat Lai (Ho Chi Minh City) to the Singapore hub, where it is transshipped onto a mainline vessel to Le Havre. Some services now call Cai Mep directly instead. [TO VERIFY:v54]
routes.origin: a factory near Ho Chi Minh City
routes.transit: ≈ 2–3 days feeder + hub dwell + ≈ 28–32 days mainline

routes.name: Guayaquil (Posorja) → Antwerp-Bruges
routes.lane: West Coast South America – North Europe
routes.detail: Bananas in 40' reefers from Ecuador's deep-water port of Posorja to Antwerp-Bruges, via the Panama Canal: about 18–22 days. Some services transship in the Caribbean. [TO VERIFY:v55]
routes.dest: the buyer's ripening centre in Belgium

compat.dry: Most boxes on this lane are reefers carrying bananas. Dry boxes carry cocoa or coffee — fine for learning.
compat.oog: Out-of-gauge cargo is rare on this lane; the journey still works, with a generator set as cargo.
compat.tank: Tanks are rare on this lane; the journey still works, with ethanol as cargo.

EXW.name: Ex Works (seller's premises)
EXW.vgmBy: the buyer's forwarder, named as shipper on the B/L — for a box it never saw
EXW.card: The buyer collects at the seller's door and does everything else, even export customs.

summary.1: The seller only makes the goods available at its premises. The buyer handles loading, export customs, freight and everything after.
summary.2: Minimum seller obligation; the buyer must clear export in a country where it may not be established. ICC suggests FCA (seller's premises) instead. [TO VERIFY:v14]

FCA.name: Free Carrier (named place: {pol} container terminal)
FCA.vgmBy: the B/L shipper — usually the seller, sometimes the buyer's forwarder
FCA.card: The seller delivers the box, cleared for export, to the buyer's carrier at the terminal.

summary.1: The seller delivers the goods, cleared for export, to the carrier chosen by the buyer at the export terminal.
summary.2: The container-friendly F-rule recommended by ICC. The parties can agree that the buyer's carrier issues an on-board B/L to the seller (useful for letters of credit). [TO VERIFY:v14]

FAS.name: Free Alongside Ship (named port: {pol})
FAS.vgmBy: the B/L shipper — usually the seller
FAS.card: Goods placed alongside the ship. Meant for bulk and break-bulk, not containers.

summary.1: The seller places the goods next to the ship. It suits bulk cargo, not containers.
summary.2: For containers, 'alongside' is effectively the terminal — FCA is the appropriate rule. [TO VERIFY:v15]

FOB.name: Free On Board (named port: {pol})
FOB.vgmBy: the B/L shipper — usually the seller, sometimes the buyer's forwarder
FOB.card: The seller is responsible until the box is on board; the buyer books the ocean freight.

summary.1: The seller pays and carries the risk until the container is loaded on the ship. The buyer books and pays the ocean freight.
summary.2: Sea-only rule. With containers, the seller loses physical control at the terminal gate but keeps the risk until loading — the reason ICC recommends FCA. [TO VERIFY:v15]

CFR.name: Cost and Freight (named port: {pod})
CFR.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
CFR.card: The seller pays the freight to the destination port, but the risk passes on board at origin.

summary.1: The seller pays the ocean freight to the destination port, but the risk passes to the buyer when the box is loaded at origin.
summary.2: Two critical points: risk on board at origin, costs to the destination port. ICC recommends CPT for containers. [TO VERIFY:v15]

CIF.name: Cost, Insurance and Freight (named port: {pod})
CIF.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
CIF.insurance: Seller — minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C) [TO VERIFY:v18]
CIF.card: Like CFR, plus basic insurance bought by the seller for the buyer.

summary.1: The seller pays the ocean freight and a basic insurance to the destination port, but the risk passes to the buyer when the box is loaded at origin.
summary.2: Risk on board at origin, costs to destination port, minimum insurance (ICC C). ICC recommends CIP for containers. [TO VERIFY:v15] [TO VERIFY:v18]

CPT.name: Carriage Paid To (named place: {pod} container terminal)
CPT.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
CPT.card: The seller pays carriage to destination; the risk passes when the box is handed to the first carrier.

summary.1: The seller pays transport to the named destination, but the risk passes when the goods are handed to the first carrier.
summary.2: The container version of CFR: risk passes at handover to the carrier (here, the origin terminal), costs to the named place. [TO VERIFY:v14]

CIP.name: Carriage and Insurance Paid To (named place: {pod} container terminal)
CIP.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
CIP.insurance: Seller — all-risks cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (A) [TO VERIFY:v18]
CIP.card: Like CPT, plus all-risks insurance bought by the seller.

summary.1: Like CPT, with the seller also buying insurance for the buyer.
summary.2: The container version of CIF. Since 2020, CIP requires higher cover (ICC A) than CIF (ICC C). [TO VERIFY:v18]

DAP.name: Delivered at Place (named place: {dest})
DAP.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
DAP.insurance: No obligation (seller carries the risk anyway)
DAP.card: The seller delivers to the buyer's door, ready for unloading; the buyer clears import.

summary.1: The seller organises and pays transport to the buyer's door. The buyer handles import customs, duties and unloading.
summary.2: If import clearance is delayed by the buyer, demurrage and detention can build up while the seller still holds the risk — allocate them in the contract.

DPU.name: Delivered at Place Unloaded (named place: {dest})
DPU.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
DPU.insurance: No obligation (seller carries the risk anyway)
DPU.card: Like DAP, but the seller also unloads at destination.

summary.1: Like DAP, but the seller also unloads the goods at the buyer's place.
summary.2: The only rule where the seller unloads at destination (formerly DAT). Risk passes once the goods are unloaded. [TO VERIFY:v14]

DDP.name: Delivered Duty Paid (named place: {dest})
DDP.vgmBy: the seller, as shipper on the B/L
DDP.insurance: No obligation (seller carries the risk anyway)
DDP.card: The seller does everything, including import customs, duties and taxes.

summary.1: The seller does everything, including import customs, duties and taxes at destination.
summary.2: Maximum seller obligation. Check that a foreign seller can legally act as importer (representation, VAT). [TO VERIFY:v26]

prompt.1: How do I travel to the port?

mode.unavailable: Other modes are not available for this terminal in this module. [TO VERIFY:v39]

body.1: Door to terminal in one go — the most common way to reach the port.
body.2: Most flexible, single handling; exposed to congestion, road weight limits and terminal appointment slots.

body.1: A river boat carrying many containers at once: cheaper per box and greener, but slower — and it leaves earlier than the port deadline.
body.2: Economies of scale and lower CO₂ per TEU; needs a barge terminal nearby, an extra handling and an earlier cut-off. [TO VERIFY:v40]

body.1: Good for long distances inland; the train runs to a rail terminal near the port.
body.2: Competitive over long distances; adds handlings at rail terminals and has its own cut-offs. [TO VERIFY:v40]

prompt.1: How do I travel from the port to the customer?

onMode.unavailable: Other modes are not available from this terminal in this module.

body.1: The quickest way to the customer's door for most deliveries.
body.2: Door delivery with appointment; road limits apply (e.g. 44 t gross for 5+ axles in France). [TO VERIFY:v13]

body.1: A river barge carries me inland, then a short truck trip reaches the door.
body.2: Barge to an inland terminal, then last-mile truck: lower cost per box over distance, more handlings. [TO VERIFY:v69]

body.1: A train takes me to an inland terminal, then a truck does the last kilometres.
body.2: Rail shuttle to an inland terminal; free time and detention keep running during the inland leg. [TO VERIFY:v69]

options.title: Merchant haulage
options.tag: The cargo side hires the truck

body.1: The cargo side hires and pays the transport company directly. The carrier's job starts at the port.
body.2: The merchant contracts and pays the haulier; the carrier's responsibility typically starts at terminal receipt (port-to-port).

body.1: The carrier organises the transport as part of its service and adds it to the invoice.
body.2: The carrier subcontracts and invoices the inland leg; its responsibility can start at the door, with an inland place of receipt on the B/L. [TO VERIFY:v43]

shipper.def: The party sending the goods and named as shipper on the bill of lading. Not always the factory: it can be a forwarder or, under EXW, the buyer's agent.

consignee.def: The party entitled to receive the goods at destination, named on the bill of lading (or the holder of a 'to order' B/L).

notify-party.def: The company the carrier informs when the cargo arrives. Being notify party gives no right to the goods by itself.

carrier.def: The shipping line that transports the container and issues the bill of lading.

freight-forwarder.def: A logistics company that organises transport for a shipper or consignee: booking, documents, customs, trucking.

nvocc.def: Non-Vessel Operating Common Carrier: books space with ocean carriers in its own name and issues its own (house) bills of lading.

booking.def: A reservation of space on a vessel and of equipment (containers) for a given route and sailing.

booking-confirmation.def: The carrier's confirmation of a booking: vessel and voyage, ports, equipment, empty pick-up depot and cut-offs.

release-order.def: The reference (or PIN) that authorises a haulier to collect a container — an empty from a depot, or a full box from an import terminal.

pin.def: A secret code the import terminal checks before releasing a full container to a truck. Some ports replace PINs with secure digital pick-up systems.

equipment-control.def: The carrier team that manages the container fleet: right empty boxes in the right place, repositioning, repairs.

depot.def: A yard where empty containers are stored, inspected, cleaned and repaired between uses.

terminal.def: The port facility where containers are received, stacked, and loaded onto or discharged from ships.

fcl.def: A container used by a single shipper for its own cargo, stuffed at its premises.

lcl.def: A small shipment consolidated with other shippers' goods in one container at a CFS.

cfs.def: A warehouse where LCL cargo is consolidated into, or taken out of, containers.

teu.def: Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit, the industry's standard measure. A 40' container = 2 TEU.

high-cube.def: A container 9'6" (about 2.90 m) high instead of 8'6": ideal for light, bulky cargo.

reefer.def: A refrigerated container with its own cooling unit, powered by electricity at terminals and on board, or by a generator set on the road.

pti.def: A technical check of a reefer's refrigeration unit before it is released for a new shipment.

set-point.def: The temperature the reefer unit is programmed to keep, given by the shipper in the booking.

genset.def: A diesel generator clipped onto a reefer's chassis or frame to power it on the road or rail.

oog.def: Cargo that sticks out beyond the normal container dimensions (height, width or length). Needs special approval, stowage and lashing.

dg.def: Hazardous cargo (flammable, toxic, corrosive…) shipped under the IMDG Code at sea, with declarations, labels and segregation rules.

imdg.def: International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code: IMO rules for packing, labelling, documenting, stowing and segregating dangerous goods at sea.

placard.def: The large diamond-shaped label on a container showing the class of dangerous goods inside.

segregation.def: Keeping incompatible dangerous goods apart in the yard and on board, as required by the IMDG Code.

stuffing.def: Loading goods into a container. The reverse is unstuffing (or stripping).

live-load.def: The truck waits while the container is stuffed. Alternative: drop and pick.

ctu-code.def: IMO/ILO/UNECE Code of Practice for Packing of Cargo Transport Units (2014): guidance on packing and securing cargo.

dunnage.def: Material used to fill gaps and protect cargo: timber, airbags, cardboard.

slac.def: 'Shipper's load, stow and count': B/L wording stating the carrier didn't see the packing and relies on the shipper's declaration.

seal.def: A numbered, single-use lock on the container door. A broken or different seal shows the box may have been opened.

iso-17712.def: International standard for mechanical container seals; class H = high security.

vgm.def: Total weight of a packed container: cargo, packaging, pallets, dunnage and the container's tare. Mandatory under SOLAS before loading.

solas.def: International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (IMO). Chapter VI covers cargo, including the VGM rule.

tare.def: The weight of the empty container, marked on its door.

csc-plate.def: Safety approval plate under the International Convention for Safe Containers, showing maximum gross mass.

weighbridge.def: A large scale on which a whole truck can be weighed.

eir.def: Record of a container's condition each time it changes hands at a gate (depot or terminal).

pre-carriage.def: Transport of the container from the shipper's premises to the port of loading.

on-carriage.def: Transport of the container from the port of discharge to the consignee.

merchant-haulage.def: The shipper or consignee (the 'merchant') arranges and pays the inland transport.

carrier-haulage.def: The carrier arranges the inland transport as part of its service and invoices it.

pre-advice.def: Advance notice to a terminal that a specific container will be delivered, so the gate can match it to a booking.

cut-off.def: A deadline set by the carrier or terminal: VGM, documentation (SI), customs, and the latest time a full box may enter the terminal (port or CY cut-off).

si.def: The shipper's data — parties, cargo, weights, seal numbers — from which the carrier drafts the bill of lading.

bl.def: The carrier's transport document: receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage and, if negotiable, a document of title.

draft-bl.def: A preliminary version of the bill of lading, sent to the shipper for checking before the final B/L is issued.

negotiable-bl.def: A B/L made out 'to order' that can be transferred by endorsement; the goods are released against an original.

sea-waybill.def: A non-negotiable transport document: the goods are released to the named consignee without presenting an original.

telex-release.def: The originals are surrendered at origin, so the carrier can release the cargo at destination without paper.

endorsement.def: Signing the back of a negotiable B/L to transfer the right to the goods to the next holder.

loi.def: A guarantee asked by a carrier to release cargo without the original B/L. Risky: P&I clubs warn against it.

hs-code.def: Harmonized System code: the international classification of goods (6 digits, extended nationally) used for duties, controls and statistics.

export-declaration.def: The customs declaration lodged by (or for) the exporter to take goods out of a country.

import-declaration.def: The customs declaration lodged by (or for) the importer to release goods for free circulation, with duties and import VAT.

customs-broker.def: A licensed specialist who prepares and lodges customs declarations for importers or exporters.

manifest.def: The list of all cargo on board a vessel, compiled by the carrier from bills of lading and filed with customs.

ens.def: Advance safety and security data on goods arriving in the EU, filed before loading for deep-sea container cargo.

ics2.def: Import Control System 2: the EU's advance cargo information system, used to risk-assess shipments before loading.

eori.def: The identification number every importer and exporter needs for customs formalities in the EU.

customs-hold.def: A block placed by customs on a container: it cannot leave the terminal until documents are checked or the box is inspected.

gate-in.def: The moment a container enters the terminal: data, seal and condition are checked and the box is handed over.

yard.def: The terminal area where containers are stacked while waiting for a ship or for collection.

rtg.def: Rubber-tyred gantry crane that stacks containers in the terminal yard.

quay-crane.def: The giant ship-to-shore crane that loads and discharges containers.

stowage-plan.def: The plan showing where every container goes on board, built from weights, destinations, DG and reefer constraints. Exchanged as EDI BAPLIE.

lashing.def: Bars, turnbuckles and twistlocks that secure containers on deck against the ship's movements.

transshipment.def: Moving a container from one ship to another at a hub port, for example from a feeder to a mainline vessel.

feeder.def: A smaller ship linking regional ports to a hub where mainline ships call.

hub.def: A large port where containers are transferred between ships (e.g. Singapore).

blank-sailing.def: A scheduled voyage that the carrier cancels; bookings are moved to another sailing.

shut-out.def: A container that misses its planned ship (no VGM, late, overbooking) and is moved ('rolled') to a later sailing.

general-average.def: An old maritime rule: when sacrifices are made to save a ship (e.g. after a fire), all cargo interests share the cost in proportion to their value.

arrival-notice.def: The carrier's message to the consignee and notify party announcing the arrival of the cargo, with charges due.

delivery-order.def: The carrier's instruction releasing the cargo to a named party once B/L, freight and charges are settled.

demurrage.def: Charge for leaving a full container in the terminal beyond the free time.

detention.def: Charge for keeping the carrier's container outside the terminal or depot beyond the free time.

free-time.def: Number of days allowed before demurrage or detention charges start, set by tariff or contract.

thc.def: Terminal Handling Charge: cost of handling the container at the terminal, charged at origin and/or destination.

baf.def: Bunker Adjustment Factor: a surcharge reflecting fuel costs.

edi.def: Electronic Data Interchange between computer systems (e.g. UN/EDIFACT). VGM = VERMAS, bay plan = BAPLIE.

pod-proof.def: The document signed by the consignee when the goods are delivered, noting any reservations.

cmr.def: The road transport document used for international road haulage in Europe under the CMR Convention.

mnr.def: Maintenance and repair of containers, usually done at depots by contractors.

incoterms.def: ICC rules defining seller's and buyer's obligations for delivery, costs and risk. Current version: Incoterms 2020. They do not transfer ownership.

ispm15.def: International standard for wood packaging: heat treatment or fumigation, shown by a stamp.

letter-of-credit.def: A bank's undertaking to pay the seller against compliant documents, often including the original B/L.

1.q: Where are the goods loaded into a full container (FCL)?

options.text: At the shipper's premises
On the ship
At the empty depot

1.explain: For FCL, the shipper stuffs its own goods at its premises; the depot only handles empty boxes.

options.text: The container's own weight plus everything inside
Only the weight of the goods
The weight of the truck and the container

1.explain: VGM = tare + cargo + packaging + pallets + dunnage. It must reach the carrier before the VGM cut-off.

1.q: Why does a container get a numbered seal?

options.text: To prove nobody opened it during the journey
To show which ship it travels on
To pay the customs duties

1.explain: The seal number is written in the documents; a broken or different seal shows the box was opened.

1.q: What happens to a container that reaches the port after the port cut-off?

options.text: It can miss its ship and wait for the next one
The ship waits for it
It is sent back to the shipper for free

1.explain: Ships keep their schedule; a late box is 'rolled' to the next sailing, often a week later.

1.q: Who usually decides which ship a container goes on, and where it sits on board?

options.text: The carrier's and terminal's planners
The truck driver
The consignee

1.explain: Planners build the stowage plan from weights, destinations and special cargo.

options.text: Moving a container from one ship to another at a hub port
Moving a container from a truck to a train
Returning an empty container to the depot

1.explain: On the Ho Chi Minh City route, a feeder brings the box to Singapore, where it is moved to the mainline ship.

1.q: At destination, what must usually happen before the consignee can collect the container?

options.text: Import customs clearance and release by the carrier
A new VGM
Nothing — the truck just picks it up

1.explain: Customs must clear the goods and the carrier must release the box (B/L, freight and charges settled).

options.text: A daily charge when the carrier's container stays outside too long
A customs penalty for wrong documents
The fee for loading the ship

1.explain: After the free days, every extra day the box stays with the customer costs money.

1.q: Do Incoterms decide who owns the goods?

options.text: No — they decide costs, risks and tasks, not ownership
Yes, ownership changes at the risk point
Only under DDP

1.explain: Ownership is set by the sales contract. Incoterms cover delivery, costs, risk and formalities.

1.q: Under {incoterm}, who books and pays the ocean freight in your journey?

options.text: The terminal

1.explain: E- and F-rules: the buyer contracts the main carriage. C- and D-rules: the seller does.

2.q: Which document is the B/L drafted from?

options.text: The shipping instructions (SI)
The booking confirmation
The VGM declaration
The export declaration

2.explain: The SI gives parties, cargo description, packages, weights and seal; the booking lacks these details.

2.q: Under SOLAS, a packed container without a VGM…

options.text: must not be loaded
can be loaded if the manifest has a weight
can be loaded with a fine
is weighed on board

2.explain: No VGM, no loading: the terminal keeps it off the load list. [TO VERIFY:v01]

options.text: from empty gate-out to full gate-in at the terminal
from booking to vessel departure
from full gate-in to loading
from discharge to delivery

2.explain: Demurrage covers time in the terminal; detention covers time outside. Tariffs vary. [TO VERIFY:v21]

2.q: A sea waybill differs from a negotiable B/L because…

options.text: it is not a document of title: cargo is released to the named consignee without an original
it is only used for reefers
it must be endorsed to the bank
it is issued before loading

2.explain: Sea waybills speed up release when no bank or onward sale needs a document of title.

2.q: Which party lodges the EU entry summary declaration (ENS) for an FCL shipment to Le Havre?

options.text: The ocean carrier (house data possibly by an NVOCC), before loading at origin
The consignee, on arrival
The exporter's broker, with the export declaration
The terminal at Le Havre

2.explain: Under ICS2 the carrier files the ENS at least 24 h before loading for deep-sea containers. [TO VERIFY:v23]

2.q: What is the main risk at a transshipment hub?

options.text: Missing the connection to the mainline vessel
A new VGM is required
The B/L is reissued
Import duties are paid there

2.explain: Feeder delays or congestion can roll the box to a later mainline sailing. [TO VERIFY:v73]

2.q: Under merchant haulage at destination, who books the truck to the consignee?

options.text: The consignee or its forwarder
The carrier
The terminal
Customs

2.explain: Merchant haulage = the cargo side organises inland transport; the carrier only releases the box.

options.text: the temperature the unit must keep, given by the shipper
the place where the reefer is plugged in
the reefer's maximum weight
the time limit for PTI

2.explain: The set point is booked by the shipper and checked at PTI and throughout the voyage. [TO VERIFY:v56]

2.q: Under CIF, where does the risk pass from seller to buyer?

options.text: On board the vessel at the port of loading
At the destination port
At the buyer's warehouse
At the export terminal gate

2.explain: Costs run to destination, but risk passes on board at origin — two critical points.

2.q: Which Incoterm does ICC recommend instead of FOB for containers?

options.text: FCA
FAS
EXW
CFR

2.explain: Containers are handed over at the terminal before loading; FCA matches that delivery point. [TO VERIFY:v15]

3.q: A customer's box is rolled because of overbooking, and the L/C requires shipment by a date that the next sailing misses. Best first action?

options.text: Inform the customer immediately with options (other service, split, amendment of L/C)
Issue the B/L with the original vessel and date
Wait until the next sailing is confirmed
Change the B/L date after loading

3.explain: Never misdate a B/L (fraud). Early transparency lets the shipper seek an L/C amendment. [TO VERIFY:v31]

3.q: The VGM received differs by 3.5 t from the booking estimate. What does the carrier rely on for stowage?

options.text: The VGM — the booking weight is only an estimate
The booking weight until the B/L is issued
The average of both
The weight on the commercial invoice

3.explain: Stowage uses the VGM; large gaps should still be queried for misdeclaration. [TO VERIFY:v01]

3.q: Seal number on the door ≠ seal number on the B/L after a customs inspection at origin. Correct handling?

options.text: Record the customs seal number and amend the documents/manifest as required
Ignore it — customs seals are always accepted
Replace the customs seal with the original number
Issue a new booking

3.explain: The new seal must be documented to avoid holds and claims at destination.

3.q: Under FOB, the box is damaged in the export yard before loading. Who bears the risk?

options.text: The seller — risk passes only on board
The buyer — it booked the freight
The carrier, always
The terminal, always

3.explain: This gap is why ICC recommends FCA for containers; carrier/terminal liability is a separate question. [TO VERIFY:v15]

3.q: A reefer alarm shows supply air +6 °C above set point mid-ocean on a frozen cargo. First step?

options.text: Reefer team checks remote data and has the crew inspect and act; inform the customer
Wait until arrival to avoid alarming the customer
Change the set point to match
Switch off the unit to reset

3.explain: Early technical intervention and documentation protect the cargo and the claim position. [TO VERIFY:v57]

3.q: Original B/L 'to order' not yet received by the consignee; cargo is in demurrage. The consignee asks for release against an LOI. Carrier position?

options.text: Release only under the carrier's LOI policy and approval — misdelivery risk is high
Release immediately: demurrage hurts everyone
Release to the notify party
Release if freight is paid

3.explain: Delivering without the original exposes the carrier to the lawful B/L holder. [TO VERIFY:v75]

3.q: General average is declared after an engine-room fire. What does the consignee need before delivery?

options.text: To provide GA security (bond and guarantee, often via cargo insurer)
Nothing if freight was prepaid
A new B/L
A new VGM

3.explain: Uninsured cargo owners must pay security themselves — a key reason to insure. [TO VERIFY:v76]

3.q: A DG tank arrives at the terminal without the DG declaration matching the booking (UN number differs). Terminal action?

options.text: Refuse or hold the box until documents and approval match
Accept it and fix the papers later
Stow it under deck to be safe
Change the UN number on the booking

3.explain: Misdeclared DG is a major safety risk; segregation and approval depend on the exact UN number. [TO VERIFY:v59]

3.q: A customer disputes detention: the box was ready but the consignee had no delivery slot. Who decides?

options.text: The tariff/contract terms; check free time, clock events and any agreed exceptions
The Incoterm
The terminal
Customs

3.explain: D&D is contractual; billing must follow the agreed events and rules. [TO VERIFY:v72]

3.q: Under CIF, the buyer finds the insurance excludes the loss that occurred. Why is this common?

options.text: CIF only requires minimum cover (ICC C)
Insurance stops at the origin terminal
Insurance is the carrier's job
CIF requires no insurance

3.explain: Buyers needing wider cover should ask for CIP (ICC A) or extra cover. [TO VERIFY:v18]
